title: Ten Percent Off Doesn't Cost You Ten Percent of Profit. It Costs More.
excerpt: Black Friday and Christmas discount codes are being locked in across the East Coast right now, and the gross profit maths behind a markdown is usually harsher than the headline percentage suggests.
content:
Black Friday is four weeks out, Christmas trading sits right behind it, and across Queensland, New South Wales and Victoria, owner-led businesses are finalising the discount codes, sale signage and promotional calendars that are meant to carry them through the final quarter of the year. The decision usually gets framed in a single, deceptively small number: ten percent off, twenty percent off, a sitewide code for the week. Set against the revenue it is expected to pull in, that number feels manageable, even conservative.

The pattern we typically see across owner-led businesses at this time of year is that the discount depth gets set based on a feel for what will drive traffic, with quiet confidence that the extra volume will more than cover the gap. Rarely does anyone work out exactly how much extra volume that actually requires before the code goes live. A discount does not come off the top of the cost base. It comes straight off the margin line, which is usually a much thinner slice of each sale than the headline price suggests, and that gap between where the discount is taken from and where it is usually imagined to come from is what makes the real cost of a markdown bigger than it looks on the surface.

None of this is an argument against discounting over the Christmas trading peak. Plenty of businesses use it well. It is an argument for knowing the number before the sale goes live, not after the quarter closes and the margin result does not match the revenue result everyone was celebrating in December.

The Maths a Discount Is Actually Doing

Take a business running a 30 percent gross margin, discounting a line by 10 percent for a Black Friday promotion. That 10 percent comes entirely out of the 30 percent margin, not out of the full sale price, so the business is giving up a third of the profit dollar on every unit sold at the discounted price. To land on the same total gross profit it would have made without running the sale at all, it needs to sell roughly 50 percent more units of that line over the promotional period, not the modest lift most owners picture when they picture a sale "bringing people in". Shift the discount to 20 percent on that same 30 percent margin and the required lift roughly doubles units sold, just to stand still on dollar profit, before any of it counts as the sale actually having worked.

Thin Margins Make the Bill Bigger, Not Smaller

The same calculation gets considerably less forgiving as the starting margin narrows, which is precisely the position a lot of hospitality, retail and trade businesses are sitting in heading into their busiest trading weeks. A business running a 15 percent margin that discounts by 10 percent needs to roughly triple its unit sales on that line to match the gross profit it would have made at full price. The deeper the discount relative to the margin it is cutting into, the steeper the volume curve climbs, and it climbs fastest for exactly the businesses that can least afford to guess wrong about how many extra customers a sale sign actually brings through the door. This is the calculation a Pricing Reset walks through line by line before a promotional calendar gets locked in, using the business's own margin and its own customer response, rather than a number set on instinct and revisited in January.

The Volume Assumption Doing the Heavy Lifting

Underneath almost every discount decision sits an assumption about how much extra volume it will actually generate, and that assumption rarely gets tested against last year's own sales data before the code goes live. A retailer in Melbourne running a sitewide 20 percent code across every product line is treating every line as equally price sensitive, when the pattern across owner-led businesses is usually the opposite: some products or services pull meaningfully more volume for a given discount, and others barely move at all no matter how deep the cut goes. Running the same markdown across the whole range means subsidising the lines that would have sold anyway at full price, while under-discounting the ones that might have actually responded to a deeper cut and genuinely lifted volume.

What to Check Before the Codes Go Live

The exercise does not need to be elaborate. Pull last year's sales by product or service line, work out the actual gross margin on each one, and run the simple division: the discount percentage over the gap between the margin and the discount. That single number is the break-even volume lift, and it is worth knowing before a discount depth is chosen rather than discovering it in the margin result three months later. Knowing which lines are genuinely price sensitive, and what each one needs to break even on a discount, is less about intuition and more about having last year's numbers broken down properly rather than treated as one blended revenue figure.

That is the kind of groundwork a fractional CFO partnership keeps current throughout the year, so the discount decision in November is based on a number rather than a feeling about what Black Friday is supposed to do. The businesses that come out of the Christmas trading peak ahead are usually the ones who already knew that number before the first code went live, not the ones recalculating it against a disappointing margin result in January.

faqs.q: How much profit does a 10 percent discount actually cost my business?
faqs.a: It depends on your starting margin, not just the discount percentage. A business running a 30 percent margin that discounts by 10 percent is giving up roughly a third of the profit dollar on every unit sold at that price, and needs about 50 percent more units sold just to match the profit it would have made without the sale at all.

faqs.q: Why do low margin businesses lose more from Black Friday style discounts?
faqs.a: The same discount eats a larger share of a thinner margin, so the extra volume needed to break even climbs sharply as the starting margin narrows. A business on a 15 percent margin discounting by 10 percent needs roughly triple the unit sales of that line to land on the same gross profit, which is a steeper ask than most promotional plans account for.

faqs.q: How do I calculate the break-even sales volume for a discount or sale?
faqs.a: Divide the discount percentage by the gap between your margin and the discount percentage. A 10 percent discount on a 30 percent margin needs a 50 percent increase in units sold (10 divided by 20) to hold the same dollar profit. Running this on your own margin by product line, rather than guessing, is the only reliable way to set a defensible discount depth.

faqs.q: Should an Australian small business run Black Friday or Boxing Day discounts?
faqs.a: There is no universal answer, and it depends on your margin, your customer base and whether the discount is likely to pull forward sales you would have made anyway at full price. What matters more than the yes or no is knowing your break-even volume before you commit to a depth and a duration, rather than setting the number on feel.

faqs.q: Should every product or service line get the same discount this Christmas?
faqs.a: Usually not. Price sensitivity varies by product and service line, and a blanket discount across the whole range typically subsidises the lines that would have sold at full price anyway while under-discounting the ones that might have genuinely responded to a deeper cut. A Pricing Reset ranks which lines are worth discounting and by how much, rather than applying one number everywhere.
